extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of world history
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style chapter recounting the political, social, and military causes that transformed the Roman Republic into the principate under Augustus, and the conditions the author deems necessary for a healthy republican state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common political idea in the minds of all men
rubrics_metrics.description: “There should be a common political idea in the minds of all men, an idea of the state thought of as the personal possession of each individual and as the backbone fact of his scheme of duties.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells argues this is the first necessary condition for a republican state. In early small Rome this could be transmitted informally within homes; in a larger country it requires organized instruction which Rome never developed. Without such a shared civic idea, moral unity and effective republic cannot be sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized teaching of history, laws, and the state's intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: The need of an organized teaching of the history, of the main laws, and of the general intentions of the state towards everyone if moral unity is to be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells contrasts the absence of such a system in Rome with the later teaching organization of Christianity (creeds, catechisms, sermons, confirmations) which supplied a permeating and correlating factor. He stresses that large polities require institutionalized civic education and that Rome lacked both the knowledge and social class to create it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal education (as the basis for republican health)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a universal education of this sort supplies only the basis for a healthy republican state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells notes universal education alone is insufficient but necessary as groundwork; it must be combined with truthful information and free discussion to support republican governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundant, prompt, and truthful information and free discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Next to education there must come abundant, prompt, and truthful information of what is going on in the state, and frank and free discussion of the issues of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He cites the modern press (imperfect though it may be) as performing these functions and contrasts this with Rome, where citizens got political facts from rumor and occasional orators and thus probably misconceived issues when voting. The author implies that a functioning press/public sphere is essential to republicanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective and comprehensible voting and civic procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Roman voting system was monstrously ineffective, contributing to misconception and the collapse of republican government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells criticizes Rome's electoral methods and the entanglement they produced; he implies that voting systems must be comprehensible and fair so citizens can exercise informed political choice, otherwise political institutions decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit or counterbalance the corrupting influence of money and concentrated wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The unforeseen invention and development of money, the temptations and disruptions of imperial expansion, and the entanglement of electoral methods weakened republican traditions by enabling men to be loyal to professions of citizenship and disloyal to its spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells highlights how wealth concentration (usurers, landgrabbers, forestallers) and monetary bribery (e.g., Jugurtha buying officials) undermined the Republic. Implicit guidance: prevent undue financial influence and economic inequalities that erode civic bonds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military loyalty and the danger of personal armies
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation of professional, landless soldiers with loyalty to commanders instead of the state undermined republican institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells describes Marius's reforms that produced soldiers whose primary interest was pay and a general's success, enabling military interventions in politics (Sulla, Caesar). He further notes the emperor remained dependent on being 'the beloved captain of his legions', so military power is both a spur to activity and a persistent threat. Implicitly, republican systems must prevent the army becoming a personal power base.
